text:
17.5 Questions to answer

Looking at Figure 17.1, which agency’s nominal budget grew the most over the years you plotted? Which shrank, or grew the least?
NSF’s FY2026 appropriation was reported as roughly flat compared to FY2024, yet in the months before that NSF terminated over 1,700 already-active grants worth about $1.4 billion. How can an agency’s total annual budget stay flat while individual grants it already promised to pay get cancelled? What does this tell you about the difference between an agency’s annual appropriation and the multi-year obligations it has already made?
How does the funding mechanism for your assigned state’s Wildlife Restoration/Sport Fish Restoration apportionment differ from how NSF or EPA award money? Based on your figure, does the state funding stream look more or less stable year-to-year than the federal agency budgets in Part 1? Does that match what you would predict from how each mechanism works?
Pick one agency and compare its line in Figure 17.1 to its line in Figure 17.2. Does adjusting for inflation change the story you would tell about that agency’s funding trend? Is there a year where the nominal and real dollar amounts tell noticeably different stories?
Look at Figure 17.5. For NASA and USDA, the research-only bar is much shorter than the entire-budget bar; for NSF, the two bars are close together. Explain why, in terms of what each agency actually spends most of its money on. Why don’t NOAA, FWS, USGS, or the Forest Service have an “entire agency budget” bar at all?
FWS’s own R&D obligations (Figure 17.4) dropped about 87% from FY2024 to FY2025, but the Wildlife Restoration/Sport Fish Restoration apportionments you collected in Part 2 come from earmarked excise tax revenue, not FWS’s regular appropriated budget. Does your class’s state-level data in Figure 17.6 show anything similar happening to the apportionments over the same period? What does that suggest about which of FWS’s funding streams is more insulated from short-term budget cuts?
Compare Figure 17.4 to Figure 17.1. USGS obligates far more research funding than FWS or the Forest Service, yet DOI as a whole (which contains all three) is one of the smaller lines in Figure 17.1. What does that tell you about the relationship between an agency’s public visibility and the size of its research budget?
If you were choosing a research area for graduate school today, would any of the trends you found here factor into your decision? Why or why not?
DOE’s row in Figure 17.3 is DOE’s entire R&D total–energy-technology research (fossil fuels, nuclear power, renewables) together with its ecological and environmental science. Compare that line to DOE BER’s line in Figure 17.4. Roughly what fraction of DOE’s total research funding actually goes to ecological/environmental science? Does that fraction surprise you, given how DOE is usually described in the news?

section: A.2 What this course is, and isn’t
text:
A.2 What this course is, and isn’t
This is book is for an ecology course, not a data-science bootcamp, and this appendix is not asking you to pretend otherwise. You are not being trained as a professional data analyst. What you are getting, most chapters, is real exposure to what practicing ecologists actually do with data and models: querying a live database, fitting a model, making a forecast, building a figure–using R code that is mostly provided to you, which you run, adapt in small ways, and interpret.
That is genuinely useful, real experience. It is not the same thing as designing an analysis from scratch or understanding the statistical theory behind it. Running a Generalized Additive Mixed Model (GAMM) and correctly reading its forecast is not the same as understanding why a GAMM works the way it does–that second thing is graduate-level material. Both are true at once: you did something real and specific, and you should not overstate what it means.
The rest of this appendix is about naming what you did accurately–specific enough to be credible, honest enough to survive a follow-up question in an interview.

A.3 The core skills you’re already building
Two things recur across nearly every chapter, as the Preface mentions: wrangling data with tidyverse-style functions (read_csv, subset, mutate, and similar), and visualizing it with ggplot2. By the time you finish this book you will have done both dozens of times, on dozens of different real datasets. That repetition–not any single chapter–is what actually makes those two skills worth naming: you can honestly say you’ve practiced them across a whole semester of varied, real data.
The table below focuses on what’s different about each chapter, on top of that recurring foundation. A small number of chapters (noted in the table) don’t use ggplot2 or tidyverse wrangling at all.

A.6 Which chapters best showcase which kind of exposure
If you want to lead with a specific kind of experience on a résumé, these are your strongest, most concrete pieces of evidence:
Live API integration / working with real-world data feeds – Funding Ecological Science (USAspending.gov, NSF Award Search), GBIF Biodiversity Data (rgbif), Traits and Physiology (BIEN). These are the most immediately recognizable to a non-academic employer: you queried a live government or scientific database, not a cleaned CSV someone handed you.
Data wrangling and reshaping (“tidy data”) – Funding Ecological Science (joining agency budgets, CPI, and state apportionment data from different sources), Traits and Physiology (long-to-wide reshaping), ForestGEO/GBIF (standardizing across sites).
Exposure to statistical modeling – Global Temperature Anomalies (GAMM/time-series forecasting), Extra-Pair Copulation (logistic regression), Metabolic Ecology (multiple regression and diagnostics). “Exposure to” is the honest frame here–you ran and interpreted these models; you were not asked to derive or fully understand the underlying theory.
Exposure to simulation and dynamical/mathematical modeling – Density-Dependence, Predator-Prey, and Carbon Cycle chapters (differential-equation modeling with deSolve); Structured Demography (matrix/eigenanalysis).
Data visualization – present in most chapters (see the core-skills note above), but Global Temperature Anomalies, Predator-Prey, and Thinking about Concepts push furthest into multi-panel, publication-style ggplot2 figures.
Comfortable working outside ggplot2/tidyverse – Structured Demography and Direct Species Interactions use base R graphics and linear algebra instead. Worth mentioning too: it shows you’re not tied to one toolkit.

A.7 Worked examples: chapter to résumé bullet
Each of these names the real tool and the real task, without claiming you designed the method yourself:
Funding Ecological Science → “Used R (jsonlite, tidyverse) to query live federal budget APIs (USAspending.gov, NSF Award Search) and join them with inflation and state-apportionment data, producing agency-by-agency funding comparisons.”
GBIF Biodiversity Data → “Used R (rgbif) to query a live biodiversity database (GBIF), assembling species-occurrence data across a latitudinal gradient and applying provided rarefaction and regression methods to examine a sampling-effort question.”
Predator-Prey (Isle Royale) → “Used a provided differential-equation model (deSolve, R) to fit 60+ years of empirical wolf-moose population data, and evaluated how well a classical ecological theory (Lotka-Volterra predator-prey dynamics) matched the real-world pattern.”
Structured Demography (Loggerhead Turtles) → “Used a provided stage-structured matrix population model (eigenanalysis, R) to identify which life stages most influence loggerhead sea turtle population growth, and interpreted the results for a conservation-management question.”
Global Temperature Anomalies → “Used a provided generalized additive mixed model, or GAMM (mgcv, R) to forecast global temperature trends with quantified uncertainty, and communicated the results through a publication-style figure.”
Compare these to a version that oversells: “Built a forecasting engine” or “developed a predictive model” implies you designed the method. “Used a provided model to…” is still specific and still names real tools and real tasks–it just doesn’t claim ownership you don’t have.

section: A.8 Being honest about what you know
text:
A.8 Being honest about what you know
A few rules of thumb for staying credible, especially in an interview:

If someone asks a follow-up question you can’t answer–“why a GAMM instead of a linear model?”, “how does the eigenanalysis actually work?”–the honest answer is some version of: “That was the method used in the course. I understand what it produced and why it mattered for the question we were asking, but I haven’t studied the underlying theory in depth.” That is a completely normal, credible thing for an undergraduate to say, and it holds up far better than getting caught overselling.
What you can honestly claim is broader than any single technique: a semester of hands-on, repeated practice reading, cleaning, visualizing, and interpreting real data, across many different real-world sources and problems. That pattern–not mastery of any one method–is the actual transferable skill, and it’s a genuinely useful thing to be able to say.

section: A.9 Building a portfolio, not just a bullet list
text:
A.9 Building a portfolio, not just a bullet list
A résumé line is words on a page; a public, working example is proof–and it’s also a natural way to show, rather than claim, the level of understanding you actually have. Your regular assignments in this course are turned in as a Word document plus a separate R script–a format that works well for grading, but isn’t something you can link to as a live, running example.
This book itself is written entirely in Quarto–a tool that combines code, narrative text, and output (figures, tables) into a single, reproducible, publishable document. You have not been asked to use Quarto for your regular assignments, and that’s a reasonable choice for a first ecology course. But if you want a portfolio piece, learning just enough Quarto to rebuild 1-2 of your best analyses as short documents–with your own explanation, in your own words, of what the code does and what you do and don’t understand about it–is a real, additional skill, and a more honest way to demonstrate your actual level of understanding than a résumé bullet alone:

Pick 1-2 analyses you understood well enough to explain to someone else.
Rebuild each as a short Quarto (.qmd) document combining your code, your figure, and your own written explanation–including, where relevant, an honest note about what you’re still fuzzy on.
Render them as a small Quarto website (a few lines of _quarto.yml configuration) and publish it for free (e.g., GitHub Pages, Quarto Pub).
Link that site from your résumé and LinkedIn profile instead of–or alongside–the bullet points above.

title: Appendix B — The Changing Landscape of Skills in Ecology
text:
B.1 Background
What should you learn when the machine already “knows” so much?
This expands on similar content in the preface.
You are learning ecology at a moment when artificial intelligence can write passable R code, summarize journal articles, and define terms like “carrying capacity” faster than you can open a textbook. That fact changes what it means to be well-trained in ecology. It does not, however, reduce the amount you need to learn — it shifts what you need to learn.
This chapter is addressed to both students and instructors. Its goal is to lay out a practical framework for thinking about which skills matter more than ever in an era of large language models (LLMs) like Claude, ChatGPT, and their successors, and which tasks can be responsibly shared with these tools. We focus on quantitative ecology because that is what this book is about, but the ideas extend broadly.
The central argument is this: AI’s fluency with ecological terminology makes it more important, not less, that you develop deep understanding of ecological mechanisms, model assumptions, and data interpretation. A machine can generate a plausible-sounding paragraph about density dependence in thirty seconds. Only a well-trained ecologist can recognize when that paragraph is subtly wrong.
crumbs: Appendices
B  The Changing Landscape of Skills in Ecology

title: Appendix B — The Changing Landscape of Skills in Ecology
section: B.2 A framework: durable skills vs. AI-augmentable tasks
text:
B.2 A framework: durable skills vs. AI-augmentable tasks
Not all skills are equally vulnerable to automation. A useful way to think about your education is to distinguish between two categories.
Durable human skills are things that require biological intuition, judgment under uncertainty, and the ability to connect mathematical abstractions to the living world. These are hard-won, slow to develop, and not reliably performed by current AI. They include:

Ecological intuition — the ability to walk into a forest, a marsh, or a dataset and notice what is ecologically interesting or surprising.
Mechanistic reasoning — understanding why a model behaves the way it does, not just that it produces a particular output.
Mathematical reasoning — the ability to follow the formal logic of a derivation, so that you can verify results, understand why an equation predicts what it does, and catch errors that sound plausible but are wrong.
Model assumption literacy — knowing what a model assumes, when those assumptions are reasonable, and what happens when they are violated.
Data literacy — the judgment to know whether data are adequate to answer a question, what biases they carry, and what they cannot tell you.
Multi-scale synthesis — connecting processes at the scale of an individual organism to patterns at the scale of a landscape or a globe.

AI-augmentable tasks are things that AI tools can do reasonably well right now, and will likely do better over time. These include:

Summarizing the main findings of a journal article.
Generating boilerplate R code for standard analyses (e.g., fitting a linear model, making a scatterplot).
Looking up definitions of ecological terms.
Drafting outlines or initial structure for a written argument.
Translating between programming languages.

Here is the key insight: AI-augmentable does not mean unimportant. You still need to understand what a linear model does and why, even if you let an AI draft the code. The danger is not that AI does these tasks — it is that you might skip the understanding that makes you capable of evaluating whether the AI did them correctly.

title: Appendix B — The Changing Landscape of Skills in Ecology
section: B.3 Why AI makes ecological understanding more important
text:
B.3 Why AI makes ecological understanding more important
This point deserves emphasis, because it is counterintuitive. You might think: if AI can write my R code and summarize my readings, I can spend less time on those things and more time on… something else. But consider what actually happens.
Suppose you ask an AI to write R code that simulates logistic population growth. The AI will almost certainly produce something that runs. But will it use the continuous-time or discrete-time model? Will it handle the time lag that makes the discrete model capable of oscillations and chaos? Will it set up the parameters in a biologically meaningful range? If you do not know enough to answer these questions, you cannot evaluate the code. You are flying blind.
Or suppose you ask an AI to explain why two competing species cannot coexist indefinitely. The AI will probably give you something that sounds like the competitive exclusion principle. But it might gloss over the specific conditions required, or fail to mention that the principle applies to a particular model with particular assumptions, and that real communities are far more complicated. The explanation will sound right. Whether it is right depends on what you, the human ecologist, know.






ImportantThe Plausibility Trap



AI-generated text about ecology is often plausible but wrong in ways that require ecological training to detect. The better the AI gets at sounding like an ecologist, the more you need to actually be one.


This is what we call the plausibility trap. AI systems are trained to produce text (and code) that looks like text (and code) produced by experts. They are not trained to be correct about the natural world. They have no field experience, no memory of watching a population crash, no intuition about whether a parameter value makes biological sense. They are pattern-matching engines — powerful ones, but without grounding in physical and biological reality.

title: Appendix B — The Changing Landscape of Skills in Ecology
section: B.4 Six categories of skills to develop
text:
B.4 Six categories of skills to develop
Let us get specific. Below are six categories of durable skills, each illustrated with examples from quantitative ecology. These are the skills this textbook is designed to build, and the ones you should invest in most heavily.

B.4.1 1. Mechanistic reasoning
Mechanistic reasoning is the ability to explain why an ecological pattern exists by tracing it back to underlying biological processes. It is the difference between saying “the population oscillates” and saying “the population oscillates because the discrete-time logistic model builds in a one-generation time lag between when crowding occurs and when its effects on reproduction are realized, and when \(r\) is large enough, this lag causes the population to overshoot and undershoot \(K\) repeatedly.”
AI can describe patterns. It can even parrot mechanistic explanations it has seen in training data. What it cannot do reliably is generate mechanistic reasoning about novel situations — situations where you are looking at a dataset or a model output that nobody has analyzed before. That is what ecologists do.
How to practice it. Throughout this book, when you are asked to run a simulation or examine data, always ask yourself: Why does this pattern exist? What mechanism produces it? Do not settle for describing what you see. Explain what causes it.


B.4.2 2. Mathematical reasoning as ecological understanding
Ecology uses mathematics to turn assumptions into predictions. When we write \(dN/dt = rN(1 - \alpha N)\) and solve for equilibrium, we are not doing math for its own sake — we are asking “what controls the long-term fate of this population?” and letting algebra answer the question. The derivation is the ecological reasoning, expressed in a language precise enough to check.
Put simply: mathematical reasoning is a form of ecological understanding — not a prerequisite for it, not a supplement to it, but one of the ways you actually come to understand how ecological systems work. When a student derives \(K = 1/\alpha\) and grasps that carrying capacity is the reciprocal of the per-capita competitive effect, they have learned something about ecology that no amount of reading prose — whether written by a textbook or an AI — will give them. The derivation is not an obstacle on the way to understanding. It is the understanding.
This matters enormously in an AI era. An AI can solve \(0 = rN(1 - \alpha N)\) and tell you \(N^* = 1/\alpha\). But can you verify that? Can you see why the equilibrium depends on \(\alpha\) and not on \(r\)? Can you explain what that means biologically — that the long-term population size depends on how strongly individuals affect each other, not on how fast they reproduce? If you can follow the two lines of algebra, these insights are obvious. If you cannot, you are taking the AI’s word for it.
The same applies at every level of model complexity in this book. When you derive the invasion criterion for two-species competition (\(K_2 > \beta K_1\)), you are discovering — through logic — the conditions under which a species can persist. When you estimate predator-prey parameters from moose and wolf population data, you are using the structure of an equation to extract biological meaning. These are not exercises in calculation. They are exercises in understanding.
The risk of skipping the math is not that you get a wrong number. It is that you lose the ability to tell whether a number is wrong. An AI can produce an answer that looks right. Only someone who can follow the formal logic can confirm that it is right — or catch where it isn’t.
How to practice it. When this book asks you to solve an equation or work through a derivation, do not skip to the answer. Follow each step and ask: what biological fact does this step reflect? When you reach the result, ask: which parameters appear, which don’t, and what does that tell me about what matters in this system?


B.4.3 3. Model assumption literacy
Every ecological model is a set of assumptions about how the world works. The exponential growth model assumes unlimited resources and no density dependence. The logistic model assumes that per capita growth rate declines linearly with population size. The Lotka-Volterra competition model assumes that the effect of one competitor on another is constant regardless of density.
These assumptions are not fine print. They are the substance of the model. When an assumption is violated, the model’s predictions can be wildly wrong. Understanding which assumptions matter and when they might be violated is one of the most important skills in ecology.






TipA Useful Habit



Before running any model, write down its key assumptions in your own words. Then ask: Which of these assumptions could be wrong for the system I am studying, and how would that change the predictions?


AI tools are particularly poor at this. They can list assumptions from a textbook, but they cannot walk outside and check whether density dependence in your study population really is linear, or whether the competitive effect of species A on species B really is constant. That judgment requires you.


B.4.4 4. Prediction before computation
One of the most effective learning strategies in quantitative ecology is to make a prediction before you run the code. What do you think will happen when you double the intrinsic growth rate? What do you expect the graph to look like when you increase carrying capacity? What will happen to coexistence if you make one species a much stronger competitor?
If you write down your prediction and it turns out to be wrong, you have learned something valuable: there is a gap between your mental model and the mathematical model. That gap is where real understanding develops.
AI eliminates this step if you let it. You can ask an AI what will happen, and it will tell you, and you will nod and move on without ever experiencing the discomfort of being wrong. Resist this. Your mistakes are the raw material of learning.
How to practice it. Every time this textbook asks you to run a simulation or modify a parameter, pause. Write down, in one sentence, what you predict will happen and why. Then run the code and compare. If you were wrong, figure out why.


B.4.5 5. Data literacy and judgment
Data literacy goes beyond knowing how to make a scatterplot or compute a mean. It includes:

Recognizing what kinds of variation are present in a dataset (measurement error, natural variation, sampling bias).
Understanding what a dataset cannot tell you because of how it was collected.
Knowing when a sample size is too small to support a conclusion.
Distinguishing correlation from causation with genuine understanding rather than just reciting the phrase.
Recognizing when an apparent pattern might be an artifact of how the data were processed.

These judgments are context-dependent and require understanding of both the statistical tools and the biological system. AI can compute a p-value, but it cannot tell you whether the study design that produced the data makes that p-value meaningful.
How to practice it. When you encounter data in this book, do not just analyze them. Interrogate them. How were they collected? What could go wrong? What alternative explanations exist for the patterns you see?


B.4.6 6. Multi-scale synthesis
Ecology spans scales from molecules to the biosphere. A well-trained ecologist can connect processes at different scales: how individual behavior gives rise to population dynamics, how population dynamics shape community composition, how community composition affects ecosystem function.
This kind of synthesis requires holding multiple frameworks in your head simultaneously and recognizing when processes at one scale constrain or enable processes at another. AI can retrieve information about any one of these scales, but it struggles to make the cross-scale connections that produce genuine ecological insight.
How to practice it. As you move through this book from individual ecology to population dynamics to community ecology to ecosystems, keep asking: How does what I learned in earlier chapters connect to what I am learning now?

title: Appendix B — The Changing Landscape of Skills in Ecology
section: B.5 Learn to distinguish between understanding and doing
text:
B.5 Learn to distinguish between understanding and doing
Writing code that plots your data is different from writing code that simulates density-dependent growth. The first you check by looking at the plot — did it do what I wanted? The second you check by interrogating the assumptions you built into the model. This distinction matters for how you think about AI and coding in this course.
Code that generates data displays, apps, or games is code that you check primarily via output. You look at or use the output and ask, did the code do what I wanted it to do? If not, attempt to troubleshoot and try again.
In contrast, code that generates mechanistic and statistical models is code that you have to understand and check primarily by evaluating assumptions that you tried to manifest in your code.
Mechanistic models are simply tools to turn assumptions into predictions, so you really need to understand how you are building those assumptions.
The output of your mechanistic model constitutes your predictions. You need to trust those predictions because they follow directly from the assumptions that you made. If the predictions seem off to you, then you need to reconsider the assumptions you made. There are three types of situations to consider:

Do you have a simple coding error? Does your code do what you intended? E.g., did you use Boolean logic correctly, or create input to a function that merely wasn’t in the right sequence?
Does your math match your ecology? How you use mathematical functions to manifest your assumptions about the biological/ecological/physical features of the world can be tricky and problems fall into two buckets: sometimes the math doesn’t do what you think it does, and other times the ecological assumptions have different consequences than you thought they would.

Are your mathematical assumptions correct? There are some convenient mathematical operations and forms that you can collect in your toolbox: functions that put a ceiling or floor on values, functions that create positive feedback loops and negative feedback loops, functions that add and those that subtract; 0th, 1st, and 2nd order products of variables.
Are your ecological assumptions correct? This is the interesting situation, where your choices of mathematical functions or parameter estimates may or may not map onto reality.

If your ecological assumptions are wrong, that is great! You’re learning something important about the world.
If your ecological assumptions are correct but the outcome is unexpected, that is great — you are discovering a consequence of your assumptions that your intuition hadn’t predicted.



This is where mathematical reasoning becomes your most important verification tool. If an AI generates model code, you can check whether it runs (easy) and whether the output looks reasonable (harder). But the deepest check is whether the mathematical structure matches the biology you intended. Does the code implement \(1 - N/K\) or \(1 - \alpha N\)? Those are equivalent — but only if \(\alpha = 1/K\). If you can’t follow that equivalence, you can’t tell whether the AI’s implementation matches your biological intention. The formal logic is the bridge between “the code runs” and “the code is right.”
How to practice it. When you encounter a place in this book where you need to use code, do not just copy some code nor ask AI for it. Ask why am I writing code?

Is it to make a graph that displays data clearly?
Is it to use mathematics to represent some biological or physical process?
Is it to perform a statistical test in which I have to understand the assumptions of that test to apply it correctly?

If you answer “yes” to no. 1, then using AI is relatively safe, but you can probably be most effective if you can work directly with any code AI spits out for you.
If you answer “yes” to 2 or 3 above, then you really need to understand what you are doing. You need to know not only that two cans of beer plus two cans of beer add up to four cans of beer, but what will happen at the party once people start drinking it.

title: Appendix B — The Changing Landscape of Skills in Ecology
section: B.6 Using AI responsibly in this course
text:
B.6 Using AI responsibly in this course
None of the above means you should avoid AI entirely. AI tools can be genuinely useful in your ecological education, but they are useful in the way a calculator is useful in a math course: they can save time on mechanical tasks, but they cannot replace the thinking that makes the tasks meaningful.
Here are some guidelines for responsible use.
Good uses of AI in ecology coursework:

Debugging R code that throws an error you do not understand.
Getting a quick refresher on R syntax (e.g., “How do I add a legend to a ggplot?”).
Generating a first draft of an outline that you then revise substantially.
Asking for alternative explanations of a concept you have already studied but find confusing.

Risky uses of AI in ecology coursework:

Asking AI to explain an ecological concept you have not yet studied yourself. (You will not be able to evaluate the answer.)
Using AI-generated code without understanding every line of it.
Asking AI to interpret your results for you. (Interpretation requires the biological context that you, not the AI, possess.)
Asking AI to write your discussion or analysis. (This is where your own ecological thinking is supposed to develop.)







WarningThe Code Comprehension Rule



If you use AI to help write R code, you should be able to explain what every line does and why it is there. If you cannot, you have not learned what you need to learn.

title: Appendix B — The Changing Landscape of Skills in Ecology
text:
B.7 A note for instructors
If you are teaching with this book, the AI landscape is shifting under your feet. Here are some principles that may help.
Design assignments that require judgment, not just output. If an assignment can be completed by pasting the prompt into ChatGPT and submitting the result, the assignment is testing the wrong thing. Assignments should require students to make predictions, evaluate assumptions, connect models to specific biological systems, and explain why a result makes ecological sense.
Make AI use transparent, not forbidden. Blanket bans on AI are difficult to enforce and send the message that AI is cheating rather than a tool. Instead, consider requiring students to document when and how they used AI, and to reflect on what they learned (or failed to learn) by using it. The goal is to develop students who can use AI wisely, not students who can pretend they do not use it.
Foreground assumptions explicitly. When teaching any model, spend time on what the model assumes and what would happen if those assumptions were violated. Use callout boxes, discussion questions, and activities that force students to engage with assumptions as substantive ecological content, not as disclaimers to be skipped.
Require prediction before computation. Build the “predict first” step into your workflow explicitly. Have students write predictions in a worksheet, a shared document, or their lab notebooks before they run code. This simple intervention creates the productive struggle that drives learning.
Use AI failures as teaching moments. Ask an AI to explain an ecological concept, and then have students identify what it got wrong. This is a great exercise in critical thinking and assumption literacy — and it demonstrates, concretely, why human expertise matters.

title: Appendix B — The Changing Landscape of Skills in Ecology
section: B.8 The skills that will define your career
text:
B.8 The skills that will define your career
The ecology profession is changing. Ecologists who graduate in the next decade will work alongside AI tools that can process satellite imagery, classify species from audio recordings, and generate code for complex statistical analyses. The value of a human ecologist will not lie in being able to do these things manually. It will lie in being able to:

Ask the right questions about the natural world.
Design studies and models that can actually answer those questions.
Recognize when a tool (AI or otherwise) is giving you the wrong answer.
Connect mathematical results to biological reality.
Communicate ecological understanding to people who need it — policymakers, land managers, communities.

These are the skills this book is designed to develop. The AI tools will change. The need for ecologists who understand the living world will not.

title: Appendix B — The Changing Landscape of Skills in Ecology
text:
B.9 Deliverables

Reflection (individual, ~300 words). Choose one of the six durable skill categories (mechanistic reasoning, mathematical reasoning, model assumption literacy, prediction before computation, data literacy, or multi-scale synthesis). Describe a specific moment in your education — in this course or another — when you were forced to use this skill. What made it difficult? What did you learn? How would the experience have been different if you had used AI to skip the hard part?
AI evaluation exercise (pairs). Pick an ecological concept covered in a previous chapter of this book (e.g., exponential growth, logistic growth, competitive exclusion, density dependence). Ask an AI to explain this concept in 2–3 paragraphs. Then, working with your partner, write a critical evaluation of the AI’s response:

What did the AI get right?
What did it get wrong, or what important nuance did it miss?
What assumptions or caveats were absent from the AI’s explanation?
Would a student who read only the AI’s response develop a correct understanding of the concept? Why or why not?

Assumption audit (individual). Choose one model from this course (e.g., the discrete-time logistic model, the Lotka-Volterra competition model). List its key assumptions. For each assumption, write one sentence explaining a real ecological situation in which that assumption would be violated, and one sentence explaining what consequence the violation would have for the model’s predictions. Do not use AI for this exercise.
Code classification (individual). Choose three coding tasks from a previous chapter of this book. For each one, classify it as primarily “check via output” (you evaluate it by looking at what it produces) or “check via assumptions” (you evaluate it by examining the ecological and mathematical logic built into the code). Write a sentence or two explaining your reasoning for each classification, and describe what you would need to understand about the ecology to evaluate the code properly.
Math as verification (individual). Ask an AI to derive the equilibrium of a model from this course (e.g., the continuous logistic, or the invasion criterion for Lotka-Volterra competition). Copy the AI’s derivation. Then, working on paper, do the derivation yourself step by step. Compare: Did the AI skip any steps? Did it make any errors? Did it explain what each step means biologically, or only algebraically? Write a paragraph reflecting on whether you could have caught an error without doing the derivation yourself.

text:
C.2 Why bother with live databases?
Every dataset in this book could have been handed to you as a clean .csv. Several of them are not, on purpose. Ecology today runs on databases that update continuously – new occurrence records, new budget lines, new trait measurements – and a large part of learning to do ecological data analysis is learning to reach into one of these moving targets and pull out exactly what you need, in a form you can trust and reproduce. A read_csv() teaches you to wrangle a table. An occ_count() or a fromJSON() call teaches you that too, plus something a static file cannot: how to ask a real, living system a specific question.

title: Appendix C — Accessing Public Ecological Databases
text:
C.4 1. Crowdsourced data: Google Sheets
Package: googlesheets4
Chapter 02 has an entire class contributing rows to the same live spreadsheet, and read_sheet() pulls whatever is currently in it, including rows that were not there yesterday.
library(googlesheets4)

d <- read_sheet(
  "https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/YOUR_SHEET_ID/edit",
  sheet = 1
)
The first time you run this in a session, R opens a browser tab and asks you to sign in to a Google account; after that it caches the authorization. If the sheet is set to “anyone with the link can view,” you can also call gs4_deauth() first to skip sign-in entirely for read-only access.






TipWhen to use a live sheet vs. a csv



A Google Sheet is the right tool when the data are still being collected – a class survey, a shared field log. Once collection is finished, export a static snapshot (File > Download > csv) into data/ so your analysis does not silently change if someone edits the sheet later.

title: Appendix C — Accessing Public Ecological Databases
text:
C.5 2. Plant trait data: BIEN
Package: BIEN
Chapter 04 queries BIEN for whole-plant height and leaf area across a species list, then reshapes the result from long to wide.
library(BIEN)

BIEN_trait_list()  # see every trait name BIEN recognizes

my_species <- BIEN_list_country(country = "Costa Rica")$scrubbed_species_binomial

my_traits_data <- BIEN_trait_traitbyspecies(
  species = my_species,
  trait   = c("whole plant height", "leaf area")
)
BIEN_trait_list() is worth running before you commit to a trait name – BIEN’s trait vocabulary is specific (e.g., “whole plant height”, not “height”), and a mismatched string returns zero rows rather than an error. There are equivalent BIEN_list_state(), BIEN_trait_traitbygenus(), and BIEN_trait_traitbyfamily() functions for narrower or broader species lists.

title: Appendix C — Accessing Public Ecological Databases
text:
C.6 3. Biodiversity occurrences: GBIF
Package: rgbif
Chapter 14 uses GBIF to compare species richness across countries and across a latitudinal gradient, entirely through live queries – no files downloaded.
library(rgbif)

palm_key <- name_backbone(name = "Arecaceae")$usageKey

richness_by_country <- occ_count(
  taxonKey   = palm_key,
  facet      = "speciesKey",
  facetLimit = 99999,
  country    = "CR"
)

effort_by_country <- occ_count(taxonKey = palm_key, country = "CR")
name_backbone() translates a taxonomic name into GBIF’s internal numeric key. occ_count(facet = "speciesKey", ...) returns one row per species, so its row count is species richness; the same call without facet returns total records, a rough proxy for sampling effort. occ_search() returns the actual occurrence records (coordinates, dates, collector) rather than just counts.






ImportantGBIF data are biased, and citing them takes an extra step



GBIF is assembled from museum specimens, herbaria, and citizen-science apps, so coverage tracks where people (and phone cameras) are, not where organisms are. Treat any pattern you find as “difference in recorded occurrences” until you have reason to think it reflects a real ecological signal.
The quick occ_count()/occ_search() calls above are fine for exploring, but are not a citable, reproducible snapshot – GBIF’s holdings change daily. For any real analysis, use occ_download() instead: it asks GBIF to assemble your exact record set and issues a DOI that pins the data and credits every contributing dataset. Cite that DOI, GBIF itself (GBIF.org 2026), and the rgbif package (Chamberlain et al. 2026).

C.7 4. Federal spending data: USAspending.gov
Package: jsonlite (talking to a REST API directly – there is no dedicated USAspending R package)
The Funding Ecological Science chapter builds agency budget comparisons this way:
library(jsonlite)

code <- "049"  # NSF's toptier agency code
url <- paste0("https://api.usaspending.gov/api/v2/agency/", code, "/")
result <- fromJSON(url)
fromJSON() fetches the URL and parses the response straight into an R list/data frame – no separate download step. USAspending.gov needs no key and has no rate limit aggressive enough to matter for classroom use, but every agency has its own numeric “toptier code” (NSF is 049), and some ecologically relevant agencies (NOAA, USGS, USFS, FWS) are sub-agencies without their own toptier code, so they have to be reached through their parent department instead.

title: Appendix C — Accessing Public Ecological Databases
section: C.9 Practical habits for working with live data
text:
C.9 Practical habits for working with live data
Save a snapshot when the data need to stay fixed, not when they are just large. The book’s own convention (see 01-computer-setup.qmd) is that hand-built or one-time reference datasets live in data/ and get read back in with read_csv(), rather than being rebuilt from a live source every render. Apply the same logic to your own project: if you need the numbers to be identical every time you re-run your script – for a report, a manuscript, a comparison over time – pull once, write_csv() the result into data/, and read that back in from then on. If you genuinely want “whatever is current right now,” call the live API every time and skip the local copy.
Respect rate limits, even generous ones. None of the five databases above will complain about the handful of queries a course assignment makes. That changes fast if you write a loop that queries thousands of times without pausing. If you are ever iterating over a long list (many species, many grid cells, many years), check the API’s documentation for a stated rate limit and add a short Sys.sleep() between calls if one is not built into the package already.
An API key, when one is required, is not optional and not something to hardcode. A few databases below (eBird, Movebank) require a free registration before you can query them at all. Store the key as an environment variable (an .Renviron file, never committed to git) rather than typing it directly into a script – the same reason you would not paste a password into code that might end up on GitHub.
Cite the data, not just the package. library(rgbif) gets you the records; it does not by itself credit the people who collected and digitized them. Most of these databases either issue a citable DOI for a specific pull (GBIF’s occ_download()) or ask for a standard attribution string (check the database’s own “how to cite” page). Get in the habit of copying that citation into your script or report at the same time you pull the data, not weeks later when you can no longer remember exactly what you queried.

title: Appendix C — Accessing Public Ecological Databases
text:
C.10 Where to look next
The five databases above are the ones this book actually puts you through. They are nowhere near the whole landscape. If you are looking for data for a class project, an independent study, or your own curiosity, these are worth knowing exist. Function names below are illustrative of what each package is for, not verified worked examples the way the sections above are – read that package’s own documentation before you build an assignment or a project around one.

NEON (National Ecological Observatory Network) – standardized, continent-scale sensor and field data (climate, soil, vegetation, organisms) from ~80 U.S. sites. R access: the neonUtilities package.
iNaturalist – citizen-science species observations with photos, often used alongside or instead of GBIF (which actually ingests research-grade iNaturalist records itself). R access: the rinat package, or GBIF directly.
eBird – bird sightings, one of the largest citizen-science datasets in existence. R access: the auk or rebird packages; querying eBird’s own API requires a free key.
Movebank – GPS and satellite tracking data for individual tagged animals. R access: the move package; many datasets require the data owner’s permission to download.
NOAA climate and ocean data – weather station records, sea surface temperature, and related long-term monitoring data. R access: the rnoaa package.
USA National Phenology Network (USA-NPN) – crowdsourced plant and animal phenology observations (leaf-out, flowering, migration) submitted through the Nature’s Notebook program, nationwide. R access: the rnpn package, an actively maintained client for USA-NPN’s own API.
LTER Network and the Environmental Data Initiative (EDI) – curated, citable datasets from the U.S. Long Term Ecological Research sites and beyond, each with its own DOI. Two different entry points depending on what you want: lterdatasampler bundles a small set of real LTER datasets already cleaned up for teaching, ready to load with no API calls at all; EDIutils is a live API client for the full EDI repository (every published LTER dataset, not just the teaching subset), for when you know roughly what you are looking for and want to query it directly.
Global Population Dynamics Database (GPDD) – long time series of population abundance across thousands of animal and plant populations worldwide, a classic source for population-ecology questions (population cycles, extinction risk, density dependence). Access has changed: the old rgpdd package talked to a database API that no longer exists and is now deprecated – do not install it. Instead, download the data directly as csv files from its permanent home at the KNB (Knowledge Network for Biocomplexity) repository, DOI 10.5063/F1BZ63Z8, and read them in with read_csv() like any other static dataset. A useful reminder that “public database” sometimes means “a DOI-cited file,” not an API.
RMBL Phenology Project (rmblphenologyproject.weebly.com) – worth knowing as a contrast to the big federated databases above: a single, long-running field program at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory in Gothic, Colorado, tracking flowering phenology in permanent plots for 150+ plant species since 1973, native bee communities since 2009, and climate/animal-arrival records since 1974. There is no live API or R package – this is one research group’s monitoring program, not a data service. Specific datasets from it have been published, tied to individual papers, through RMBL’s own data catalog (rmbl.org) and through general-purpose repositories like OSF and Dryad. If a project idea points you toward a single well-known field site or long-term study rather than a global database, this is the kind of place you end up: search the study’s own site or the paper’s data-availability statement for a repository link and a DOI, rather than expecting a package.
Dryad and other data repositories – data deposited alongside individual published papers, useful when you want the exact dataset behind a specific result rather than a whole live database.

C.11 A note on why some of this book’s chapters use live queries and others use data/
You may notice this book is inconsistent, on purpose: some chapters query a live database every time they render, and others read a fixed .csv from data/. That is not sloppiness – it reflects the same choice described in “Practical habits” above, made deliberately for each chapter. A chapter built around teaching how to query a live source (BIEN, GBIF, USAspending, NSF) leaves the query live, so what you see is really happening in real time. A chapter that needed a small, specific, one-time dataset (inflation figures, a curated budget table) built it once and saved it to data/, so the numbers in the book do not drift out from under the prose describing them. When you design your own project, make that same choice deliberately, not by default.
